0.title: When the Heat Rises
0.essay:
The keys will not turn up. The children are fighting again. A car cuts in front of you on the motorway. Someone at work takes the credit for your idea. Before you have decided anything, something hot rises in your chest and comes out of your mouth, or goes cold and silent behind your eyes. If you know that moment, this study is for you.

A familiar fire

Anger is one of the commonest feelings there is, and one of the most confusing for Christians. We know that “the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God” (James 1:20). Yet the Bible also tells us that God is angry, and that Jesus was angry. Is anger always sin? Why does it flare so fast and linger so long?

Where we are going

This study does not offer a technique for keeping the lid on. It looks honestly at the many shapes anger takes, from the quick snap to the long freeze. It sets our anger beside God’s holy and patient anger, and beside the anger of Jesus. It digs beneath the heat to the desires that feed it, listens to God’s gentle question to an angry prophet, and stands at the cross, where God’s just anger against sin fell on his own Son. It ends with practical wisdom for the hot moment and for the repair afterwards, including what to do when anger has become abuse.

Other studies come at this subject from other sides. The Tongue looks at angry words, Forgiveness & Reconciliation at forgiving those who wrong us, Christian Parenting at not provoking our children, and Fighting Sin & Temptation at the battle with sin in general. Handling Conflict looks at difficult people and peacemaking. This study stays with the heart that gets angry.

The chapters

Many Kinds of Heat; Holy Anger and Ours; What Lies Underneath; “Do You Do Well to Be Angry?”; Where Anger Was Spent; and In the Hot Moment and Afterwards.

For reflection

When did you last feel angry? What shape did it take: a raised voice, a muttered word, or a long silence? Who was on the receiving end?

1.title: Many Kinds of Heat
1.essay:
Anger does not always shout. Sometimes it slams a cupboard door. Sometimes it sighs loudly. Sometimes it goes quiet for three days. Before we can deal with anger, it helps to recognise the shapes it takes in us.

Snapping at home

For many people anger is at its worst with the people they love most. We are patient with colleagues and polite to strangers, then snap at a husband over the dishwasher or at a child who is slow putting on shoes. Home is where we are tired, where we feel safe enough to let go, and where our plans are most often interrupted. It is also where anger does the most damage, because it lands on people who cannot easily walk away, and on children who are still learning what love looks like.

Irritation

Some anger never reaches a raised voice. It hums along all day as irritation: at the slow queue, the loud chewing, the colleague who starts every sentence with “to be honest”. Irritation feels too small to matter. But Paul, describing love, says it “is not irritable or resentful” (1 Corinthians 13:5). A thousand small irritations shape a person as surely as one great outburst, and the people around us feel every one.

Simmering resentment

Resentment is anger that has been kept. It goes back over an old wrong, real or imagined, and tastes it again. It keeps a file. It can live for years under a pleasant surface: the relative never forgiven for something said at a wedding, the manager who passed you over. Hebrews warns against any “root of bitterness” that “springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled” (Hebrews 12:15). Roots grow out of sight, and they spread.

Road rage and the faceless enemy

Put a gentle person behind a steering wheel and something can change. The other driver is no longer a man with a sick child in the back seat. He is an obstacle and an insult. The car gives us a kind of anonymity, and anonymity loosens restraint. The same thing happens online, where people type what they would never say to a face. Road rage is worth noticing because it shows that the anger was there all along. The car only took the lid off.

Cold anger

Not all anger is hot. Some people never shout. They withdraw. They go silent, answer in single words, become very busy, and punish with coolness. This can look like self-control, and is sometimes praised as such. But silence used as a weapon is still anger. It still says, “You have wronged me, and you will pay.” Cold anger is harder to name than hot anger, and so it often lasts longer.

Jesus’ words reach both kinds: “everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5:22). He traced murder back to the heart, and the heart can be furious without making a sound.

The first angry man

Anger appears early in the Bible. When God accepted Abel’s offering and not his, “Cain was very angry, and his face fell” (Genesis 4:5). God came to him with a question: “Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen?” (Genesis 4:6). Then a warning: “sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is for you, and you must rule over it” (Genesis 4:7). Cain did not rule it. A few verses later his brother was dead.

The story is not told to make us think every irritable person is a murderer. It is told to show us what anger is like. It crouches. It waits at the door of the heart, and it wants more than it first asks for. A sulk becomes a grudge, and a grudge becomes cruelty. Yet notice that God spoke to Cain before he acted. Even then, the Lord was reasoning with him and holding out a way back.

An example

A mother of three is known at church as calm and kind. At home, by six o’clock, she is often shouting. One evening her eldest, aged nine, says quietly, “You’re always cross with us.” It stings because it is nearly true. She lies awake wondering how the patient woman everyone else sees and the woman her children see can be the same person.

Honest, not hopeless

Seeing our anger clearly is uncomfortable. But we cannot bring to God what we will not admit is there. The good news, which the rest of this study unfolds, is that God does not leave angry people alone at the door. He comes to us, as he came to Cain, and in Christ he does far more than warn.

For reflection

Which of these shapes of anger do you recognise most in yourself: snapping, irritation, resentment, road rage or cold withdrawal? Who usually bears the brunt of your anger? Is there a grievance you have been keeping on file? How would you answer God’s question to Cain, “Why are you angry?”

2.title: Holy Anger and Ours
2.essay:
The Bible speaks of God’s anger more often than many people expect. That can be frightening. But it also helps us, because when we see what holy anger looks like, we see more clearly what ours so often is not.

God is angry, and slow to anger

When the Lord showed Moses his glory, he described himself as “merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). Slow to anger. His anger is real: “the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men” (Romans 1:18). But it is never quick-tempered, never petty and never out of control. He waits, he warns, he sends prophets. “He will not always chide, nor will he keep his anger forever” (Psalm 103:9).

God’s anger is holy. It is not a mood or a bruised ego. It is the settled opposition of perfect goodness to everything that spoils what he made. A God who looked at cruelty, abuse and lies and felt nothing would not be good. His anger is the other side of his love: he is angry at what destroys the people and the world he loves.

God’s anger is also just. Nahum says in one breath that “The LORD is slow to anger and great in power, and the LORD will by no means clear the guilty” (Nahum 1:3). He never punishes more than is deserved and never acts on half the facts. Our anger does both.

Jesus was angry

The gentlest man who ever lived was sometimes angry. In the temple, “making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen. And he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables” (John 2:15). The worship of his Father had become a marketplace. His disciples remembered the words, “Zeal for your house will consume me” (John 2:17).

On another day, in a synagogue, a man with a withered hand stood before him, and the religious leaders watched to see if Jesus would heal on the Sabbath so they could accuse him. “And he looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart, and said to the man, ‘Stretch out your hand.’ He stretched it out, and his hand was restored” (Mark 3:5).

That anger was mixed with grief. It was aimed at a hardness that kept a suffering man from help. And it turned into action that did good: he did not insult them; he healed the man. It was not about himself. When Jesus himself was mocked and beaten, “he did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2:23). He was angry when his Father was dishonoured and the weak were wronged, and silent when only he was insulted. We tend to be the other way round.

Be angry and do not sin

So anger is not always sin. Paul writes, “Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil” (Ephesians 4:26–27). There are things that ought to stir a Christian: a child harmed, the poor exploited, a good name ruined by lies. Not to care would be a failure of love.

But Paul puts a fence round it at once, and a few verses later he adds, “Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you, along with all malice” (Ephesians 4:31). The anger that may be right for a moment becomes wrong when it settles in, spreads and hardens into bitterness and malice.

The anger of man

James is blunt: “let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God” (James 1:19–20). Even when the cause is just, our anger is usually mixed: part concern for what is right, part wounded pride, part wish to win. It exaggerates and forgets its own faults. When Nathan told King David about a rich man who stole a poor man’s lamb, “David’s anger was greatly kindled against the man” (2 Samuel 12:5). He was quite right to be angry, and quite blind. “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7).

Can our anger be righteous?

Christians answer this differently. Some, pressing James 1:20, say that in sinners nearly all anger is sin, and we should almost never call ours righteous. Others, many Christian counsellors among them, see anger as a neutral emotion, a signal that something matters, and say the only moral question is what we do with it. The first view takes seriously how easily we fool ourselves; the second, that God made us to care about right and wrong.

This commentary’s view: anger is never quite neutral, because it is always a judgment that something is wrong and someone is to blame. It is right when that judgment is true and the response is in proportion, controlled and aimed at good, as Jesus’ was. Christians can feel such anger, and sometimes should. But in us it is never pure, and it sours quickly. So we should be slow to call our anger righteous, quick to examine it, and quicker still to turn it into action that helps rather than words that wound.

An example

A retired teacher is furious when she learns that a frail neighbour has been cheated by a builder. She helps the neighbour report it and prays for the builder. In the same week she is furious that her son forgot her birthday, and that anger sits in her for days. Setting the two side by side, she can see which anger was about love and which was about her.

For reflection

Which surprises you more: that God is angry, or that he is slow to anger? What strikes you about Jesus’ anger in Mark 3:5? Think of a time you felt your anger was righteous: was it in proportion, controlled, and aimed at good? Why might Jesus have been silent when insulted but angry when others were wronged?

3.title: What Lies Underneath
3.essay:
Anger feels as if it comes from outside. He made me angry. The traffic made me angry. But Scripture keeps turning our eyes inward. Another person may strike the match, but what catches fire was already there.

James asks a question

“What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel” (James 4:1–2). James does not deny that other people do wrong. He points to something deeper: desire. I want something. I am not getting it. Someone is in the way. The heat rises.

Try it on your last flash of anger. I wanted a quiet evening, and the children were loud. I wanted to arrive on time, and the car in front was slow. I wanted to be listened to, and I was interrupted. Underneath almost every angry moment there is a sentence that begins, “But I wanted …”

Good things made ultimate

The desires are often good ones: peace, order, respect, rest, a happy family. The problem is not wanting them. It is wanting them so much that they rule us. When a good thing becomes a must, something I cannot live without, then whoever blocks it becomes my enemy. The Bible’s word for a good thing that takes God’s place is an idol, and anger is often the alarm that sounds when an idol is threatened. That is why we can be so furious over things that, a week later, we can hardly remember.

Some common roots

Control. “Things must go the way I planned.” Interruptions, delays and other people’s choices feel like attacks. Many angry people are not cruel. They are people who need life to be orderly, and life rarely is.

Entitlement. “I deserve better than this.” In Jesus’ parable, when the prodigal came home, the elder brother “was angry and refused to go in” (Luke 15:28). His complaint was, “these many years I have served you … yet you never gave me a young goat” (Luke 15:29). He thought his father owed him. Entitlement turns every disappointment into an injustice.

Fear. Much anger is fear wearing armour. The father who shouts when his teenager comes home late is often a frightened father. The person who flares up at criticism may be afraid of being found out. Anger feels stronger than fear, so we reach for it.

Pride. Haman had wealth, sons, promotions and a place at the queen’s banquet, yet when Mordecai would not bow to him, “he was filled with wrath” (Esther 5:9). He told his wife and friends, “Yet all this is worth nothing to me, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king’s gate” (Esther 5:13). One man’s refusal to honour him outweighed everything else he had. The study The Fear of Man explores this craving for honour more fully.

The heart that excuses itself

We rarely see these roots for ourselves. “All the ways of a man are pure in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the spirit” (Proverbs 16:2). In the moment our anger always feels justified. We are the hero of our own story and the other person is the villain. That is why we need God to search us: “Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts!” (Psalm 139:23). And it is why we need other people, a husband or wife, a friend, a pastor, who can tell us kindly what they see.

Temperament explains, but does not excuse

Some of us are quicker to anger by nature or upbringing. A home full of shouting teaches a child that shouting is how problems are solved. Tiredness, hunger, pain, stress, hormones, alcohol and some illnesses all shorten the fuse. These things are real and worth attending to, and the last chapter says more about when to see a doctor. But they explain anger; they do not excuse it. Paul lists “fits of anger” among the works of the flesh (Galatians 5:20), and “patience” and “self-control” among the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23). The Spirit does not only calm us down. He changes what we love, and that changes what makes us angry.

An example

A businessman notices that he loses his temper most when his plans are overturned: a cancelled flight, a late delivery, his wife changing the weekend arrangements. Talking it through with a friend from church, he sees that what he calls “being organised” is really a deep need to be in control. When he was a boy, his father’s drinking made home chaotic and frightening, and he decided that he would never feel that helpless again. Seeing this does not fix him. But it shows him what to pray: “Lord, you are in control, and I am not. Teach me to trust you with my plans.”

Finding the root is a mercy

None of this is meant to make us wallow. You cannot kill a weed by cutting off the leaves, and you cannot change anger only by managing its outbursts. The root is exactly what the gospel reaches. When Christ becomes our deepest treasure, other good things lose their stranglehold. A ruined evening is no longer the end of the world, because our world is no longer built on evenings going well.

For reflection

Think of your last angry moment. What did you want that you did not get? Which root most often lies under your anger: control, entitlement, fear or pride? What good thing might have become a “must” for you? Who could help you see your own heart more clearly?

4.title: “Do You Do Well to Be Angry?”
4.essay:
The book of Jonah ends not with a full stop but with a question. An angry prophet sits outside a city, sulking, and God gently asks him to look at his anger. It is one of the most tender passages about anger in the Bible.

Angry at mercy

Jonah was sent to Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, a cruel enemy of his people. He ran the other way. After the storm and the great fish he went and preached, and the whole city repented. “God relented of the disaster that he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it” (Jonah 3:10). Most preachers would have been overjoyed. “But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry” (Jonah 4:1).

His prayer tells us why. “I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster” (Jonah 4:2). Jonah quotes God’s own description of himself back to him as a complaint. He was angry that God was not angry enough. The enemies he wanted punished had been shown mercy.

There is some Jonah in most of us. We want mercy for ourselves and justice for those who hurt us. A good deal of our anger at other people is really anger that God has not yet dealt with them as we would like.

Angry enough to die

Jonah went further: “please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live” (Jonah 4:3). God did not shout or strike him down. He asked a question: “Do you do well to be angry?” (Jonah 4:4). He invited Jonah to step back and look at what was happening inside him.

Jonah did not answer. He sat outside the city to see what would happen. God made a plant grow to shade him, and “Jonah was exceedingly glad because of the plant” (Jonah 4:6). Then God sent a worm and a scorching wind, the plant withered, and Jonah again wanted to die. God asked again whether he did well to be angry for the plant, and Jonah said, “Yes, I do well to be angry, angry enough to die” (Jonah 4:9).

Notice how anger shrinks the world. Jonah grieved for a plant and felt nothing for a city. Anger turns people into obstacles and small losses into disasters. Notice too where it led him: to despair. If anger, or the hopelessness that can follow it, has ever brought you to wish you were dead, please do not sit alone with it as Jonah did. Get help now: call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America) or a crisis line (Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, 988 in the United States), and tell someone you trust.

God’s last word

“You pity the plant, for which you did not labor, nor did you make it grow, which came into being in a night and perished in a night. And should not I pity Nineveh, that great city, in which there are more than 120,000 persons who do not know their right hand from their left, and also much cattle?” (Jonah 4:10–11). The book stops there. We never hear Jonah’s reply. The question is left with us.

Look at the patience of God with this angry man. He had every right to be angry with Jonah. Instead he gave him shade, reasoned with him and asked him questions. The God who is slow to anger was slow with Jonah’s anger too. And Jesus later said of himself, “something greater than Jonah is here” (Matthew 12:41). Jonah sat outside a city hoping for fire. Jesus wept over Jerusalem, the city that would reject him, and went into it to die for sinners.

Angry at God

Jonah’s anger was aimed at God. Many Christians know that feeling, though few admit it: anger at a death, an illness, an unanswered prayer.

The Psalms show a better way than Jonah’s sulk. “How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?” (Psalm 13:1). “Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord?” (Psalm 44:23). “O LORD, why do you cast my soul away? Why do you hide your face from me?” (Psalm 88:14). These are laments, and God put them in his book. He invites us to “pour out your heart before him” (Psalm 62:8).

The difference between lament and Jonah is direction. Jonah ran from God and then sat with his back to him. The lament psalms run to God and keep talking to him, even in protest. Lament is anger that still believes God is there and still hopes in him. Psalm 13 begins with “How long?” and ends, “But I have trusted in your steadfast love” (Psalm 13:5). God has never wronged us, so he needs no forgiveness from us. But he can hold our honest pain. Jesus himself prayed a lament from the cross: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34). The study Disappointment & Waiting says more about unanswered prayer.

An example

A man in his fifties lost his wife to cancer after two years of prayer. He still goes to church, but he feels a cold anger towards God that he has told no one. His pastor suggests he read Psalm 88 aloud and then write his own psalm. He writes three angry pages. At the bottom, almost against his will, he writes, “But you are still the only one I can talk to.” It is the first time in months he has prayed.

For reflection

Have you ever been angry that someone else was shown mercy? Where do you see Jonah’s shrunken world in your own anger? How would you answer God’s question, “Do you do well to be angry?”, about the last thing that made you angry? Is there anger at God that you need to bring to him honestly, as a lament?

5.title: Where Anger Was Spent
5.essay:
Our anger keeps accounts. It wants wrongs paid for. The gospel does not tell us that wrongs do not matter. It tells us where they have been dealt with. At the cross, God’s just anger against sin was not cancelled or ignored. It was poured out on his own Son.

We were the ones he was angry with

Before we think about the anger we feel towards others, we have to face the anger God rightly had towards us. Paul says we “were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind” (Ephesians 2:3). God’s anger at sin is not only for Nineveh, or for the person who hurt us. It was against us. Then come two of the most beautiful words in the Bible: “But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ” (Ephesians 2:4–5).

The cup

In Gethsemane Jesus prayed, “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39). The prophets spoke of “the cup of his wrath” (Isaiah 51:17), the judgment God’s people deserved. Jesus was about to drink it. “He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace” (Isaiah 53:5).

Paul calls Jesus “a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25): a sacrifice that turns God’s anger away by bearing it. This was “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). God did not pretend sin was nothing. He was just, because sin was punished, and merciful, because it was punished in his Son and not in us. “In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 4:10).

So Paul can say, “Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God” (Romans 5:9). For everyone who trusts in Christ, God’s anger is spent. Not a drop is left. Stop and wonder at that. The holy God, who had every right to be angry with us, took his own anger on himself in the person of his Son, and turned to us with open arms. The one who could have been our judge became our substitute.

Never avenge yourselves

This changes how we carry the wrongs others do to us. Paul writes, “Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, ‘Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord’” (Romans 12:19).

Paul assumes there are real wrongs that deserve repayment. But he moves the account onto God’s desk. Every wrong done to you will be dealt with. Either it was paid for at the cross, if the one who wronged you turns to Christ, or it will be judged with perfect justice on the last day. Nothing will be overlooked. You do not have to be the judge. You can put the file down.

This is how Jesus himself endured, “entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). And on the cross he prayed for the men who nailed him there: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34).

Letting go of resentment

Resentment says, “I will not let this go until they pay.” The gospel answers: they will pay, or Christ already has. Either way, it is not ours to collect. And those of us who have been forgiven an enormous debt hear the king in Jesus’ parable asking, “should not you have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?” (Matthew 18:33).

Letting go of vengeance does not mean saying the wrong was fine, trusting someone again at once, or keeping quiet about a crime. God has given governments and courts to restrain evil (Romans 13:4), and going to them is not revenge. It means giving up the private wish to see the person hurt, and the inner rehearsal of their punishment. The study Forgiveness & Reconciliation sets out what forgiveness is and is not. The point here is simpler. At the cross we see that God takes wrong more seriously than we ever could, so we do not have to carry the weight of making sure he does.

Overcome evil with good

Paul goes on: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21). Freed from the work of vengeance, our energy can go into doing good, even to those who have hurt us. That is not weakness. It is the strength of someone who knows the account is safe in God’s hands.

An example

A woman was cheated by her brother out of her share of their parents’ estate. For eight years she went over it in her mind most nights. Hearing a sermon on Romans 12, she realised she had made herself his judge, and that she was the one serving the sentence. She did not suddenly feel warm towards him. But she prayed, “Lord, he is yours to deal with. I give you the file.” She noticed that the next anniversary of their mother’s death passed without the usual sleepless night. Some months later she sent him a short, kind card.

For reflection

How does it change your anger to remember that you were once among the “children of wrath”? What does the cross show about whether God takes wrong seriously? Is there someone you have been trying to make pay? What would it look like to leave that with God, and to “overcome evil with good” this week?

6.title: In the Hot Moment and Afterwards
6.essay:
The gospel is not only for quiet times. It is meant for the kitchen at six o’clock, the traffic jam and the tense meeting, and for the hours afterwards. Here is some practical wisdom, offered not as rules to earn God’s favour, but as ways to live out of the peace Christ has already made.

Know the warning signs

Anger usually announces itself in the body first: a hot face, a tight jaw, a racing heart, a raised voice. Learn your signs, and learn your danger times: late afternoon, when you are hungry or tired, certain subjects, certain people. “Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a hasty temper exalts folly” (Proverbs 14:29).

Slow down

“A fool gives full vent to his spirit, but a wise man quietly holds it back” (Proverbs 29:11). Holding back is not pretending you are not angry. It is refusing to let anger choose your words. Breathe and lower your voice. A few seconds of delay can change a whole evening.

Step away, and come back

“The beginning of strife is like letting out water, so quit before the quarrel breaks out” (Proverbs 17:14). It is often wise to say, “I’m getting angry, and I don’t want to say something I’ll regret. Give me ten minutes, and then let’s talk.” Then come back. Stepping away for a while is wisdom; staying away to punish is cold anger by another name.

Pray in the moment

A short prayer is enough: “Lord, help me.” Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come to him, “for I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). He is gentle with angry people who come to him, and he can make us gentle too.

Answer softly

“A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1). Tone carries as much as words. The study The Tongue has more on speaking well when tempers are high.

Afterwards: repair

“Do not let the sun go down on your anger” (Ephesians 4:26). Do not leave the damage overnight if you can help it. Jesus says that if you remember your brother has something against you, “First be reconciled to your brother” (Matthew 5:24). Go back and apologise. Name what you did, without a “but” and without “you made me”: “I was wrong to shout at you. I’m sorry. Will you forgive me?” Do it with children too; it shows them what grace looks like. Confess it to God as well, with confidence: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

When you are the one who was wronged, be ready to forgive, “as the Lord has forgiven you” (Colossians 3:13), and when the anger returns, hand it back to God again. Then look underneath, using the questions in the third chapter: what did I want so badly?

When anger becomes abuse

Some anger crosses a line. Shouting that makes others afraid, threats, smashing things, controlling money or movements, constant belittling, any hitting, pushing or restraining: this is abuse, not just “a temper”.

If you are on the receiving end, your safety comes first. You are not required to stay in danger, and leaving to escape abuse is not the separation Scripture forbids. If you are in danger, call the emergency services. Speak to someone you trust, and contact a domestic abuse helpline (in the UK, the National Domestic Abuse Helpline on 0808 2000 247; in the United States, the National Domestic Violence Hotline on 1-800-799-7233). Abuse should be reported to the authorities, and where children are at risk, report it at once. Church leaders should support you and help you get safe, never press you to keep quiet. The study Divorce & Remarriage discusses these hard cases.

If you are the one whose anger frightens others, be honest about it. Tell your pastor or a mature Christian everything, and accept their help and their accountability. Join an anger management course or see a qualified counsellor. Accept the consequences, including others’ need for distance. Real repentance does not demand that trust be restored at once. God’s grace is for you too, but it is never a cover for continuing harm.

When to see a doctor

Constant irritability can be a sign of depression, anxiety, trauma, chronic pain, poor sleep, hormonal changes or other illness, and alcohol makes most anger worse. If your anger seems out of proportion and out of character, see a doctor. Getting help from a doctor or counsellor, or taking medicine that is prescribed, is no failure of faith. The study Depression & the Christian says more.

An example

A father realises he snaps at his teenage son almost every evening. He agrees a plan with his wife. When he feels the heat rising, he says, “Give me five minutes,” walks round the garden and prays. Then he comes back and talks. The first time he apologises properly, “I was wrong to speak to you like that. Will you forgive me?”, his son looks at him in surprise and says, “Yeah. Thanks, Dad.” It is the longest conversation they have had in weeks.

Growing slowly

Patience is fruit, and fruit grows slowly. You will fail again. When you do, go back to the cross, where God’s anger against your sin has already been spent, and start again. “Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city” (Proverbs 16:32). Little by little the Spirit makes God’s children like their Father: slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love.

David Powlison’s Good and Angry is a wise and practical book on this subject.

For reflection

What are your warning signs, and your danger times? Which practice would help you most in the hot moment? Is there someone you need to go back to and apologise to today? If anger in your home has become frightening, who will you speak to this week?
